methodology.primary: Biblical passages listed with each Gospel/Acts episode are primary narrative sources. The published sequence is a Gospel harmony, not a separately dated GPS reconstruction.
methodology.scope: First-pass editorial and machine-assisted reference/location screening of 79 episodes and 35 dossiers, now supplemented by individually written biblical reading context for all 79 entries and three additional bounded historical/textual research issues. Corrected particular overclaims and recorded disputes. NOT independent specialist historical, textual or archaeological certification. This is not a claim of independent scholarly certification.

sourceTypes.scripture: Canonical Gospel/Acts narrative cited for each episode; text is opened in authorised reader.
sourceTypes.historical: External archaeological or academic reference; proves only its stated archaeological/historical claim.
sourceTypes.tradition: Later veneration or a candidate location, not independent proof of an episode.

methodology.reviewer: Scripture Trails editorial - AI-assisted initial review; independent subject-matter review pending
methodology.translationPolicy: ESV, NASB20, NIV and NKJV are available reader editions. Differences in translation, verse numbering and ancient manuscripts require examination in context.
methodology.voteAndSourcePolicy: OpenBible.info cross-reference votes express source-seeded and community-ranked relevance, not scholarly confidence. A missing secondary literature link is a research gap, not proof or disproof of an event. Biblical references are primary witnesses to their textual claims, not independent archaeological verification.

issues.description: Luke and Matthew provide different amounts of detail between presentation, Egypt and Nazareth. The combined timeline is interpretative.
John 2 and the Synoptic final-week temple scenes cannot be asserted to be two independently proved actions.
Luke 4 and Mark 6 place hometown synagogue narratives differently; identity and sequence of the encounters need specialist comparison.
Luke 5 and Mark 1 may represent differently framed reports; avoid a single precise date for all details.
Mark 5:21 specifies the lakeshore but does not name Capernaum for the encounter.
The Bethsaida designation in Luke and the deserted place framing in the parallel Gospels do not yield a single surveyed feeding point.
Caesarea Philippi district and surrounding villages are named; a specific urban address is not.
Luke names the Samaria/Galilee border corridor; no exact road, border-crossing point or chronology is stated.
The ESV notes that John 7:53-8:11 is absent from the earliest manuscripts; this event cites 8:12 onward rather than silently treating the disputed pericope as part of the feast teaching.
John 12 and Mark 14/Matthew 26 may be parallel accounts or distinct events; the composite map cannot prove additional trips.
Arrival near Bethphage is named; the village from which the donkey was brought is not independently identified.
Luke describes approach, while Mark and Matthew describe departure from Jericho; location and narrative grouping are qualified.
John and the Synoptics relate the final supper to Passover differently, and no uncontroversial harmonised date is fixed.
Jerusalem and Golgotha are named in the text; exact trial, crucifixion and tomb coordinates are not independently proven by modern commemorative buildings.
Appearance accounts do not yield one undisputed, continuously dated route; John 20:19-29 includes a later gathering involving Thomas.
Gerasenes/Gadarenes/Gergesenes are variant geographical readings; the marker remains a region, not a verified landing site.
El-Araj and et-Tell remain competing Bethsaida candidates; excavations must not be treated as proof of the Gospel event.
The biblical name Emmaus is clear but its modern identification remains contested.

Mark 6:45 gives Bethsaida as an intended destination, whereas 6:53 gives Gennesaret as the landfall. John 6:17 uses Capernaum as the direction of travel. The text distinguishes intention from arrival; a physical course or single harmonisation is not established. A published narrative-critical article examines the Markan destination tension.

Luke 2:1-2 places Jesus' birth in the setting of an imperial census associated with Quirinius, while Matthew 2:1 begins in the time of Herod the Great. Conventional dates for the Quirinius census and Herod's death create a significant historical chronology question. Published scholarship offers competing readings, but this itinerary does not assert a resolved year or a proved earlier census.

Several early witnesses and critical modern Bible editions end Mark's continuous narrative at 16:8 or bracket 16:9-20. Many other manuscripts transmit the longer ending. The resurrection-stop reference deliberately uses Mark 16:1-8, rather than implying Mark 16:9-20 has no textual dispute. Manuscript age and transmission require specialised evaluation.

Luke 24:51-52 includes readings with different manuscript support concerning the ascension and worship, discussed in textual criticism alongside Acts 1. The current reader passage is a translated canonical text, not a comprehensive manuscript comparison. The broad Bethany/Mount of Olives identification must not be turned into exact coordinates or a synchronised hour.

literatureUpdate.method: Follow-up editorial linking of academic discussions of textual arrangement to specific unresolved Gospel parallels. These links establish the interpretative issue, not the historicity or identity of either episode. The first-pass screening remains dated 26 October 2026; no external specialist review or new archaeological verification was performed.
notes: Nazareth rejection: the relative literary placements of Luke 4 and Mark 6/Matthew 13 are reviewed in published biblical scholarship.
Fishermen's calling: Mark places calling before the Capernaum synagogue; Luke describes the call after its Capernaum teaching. Both catalogue entries now point to the open ordering issue.

referenceIntegrity.method: Automated canonical-reference boundary checks were added for the existing Scripture citation registers using local Protestant 66-book KJV-style verse counts. This validates reference addressability in that numbering scheme, not manuscript variants, translation equivalence, historicity, or scholarly review.
coverage: Historical city study passage registers, timelines, evidence cards and disputed-site links
referenceIntegrity.limitations: Some Bible editions, textual traditions and psalm titles use different versification. The checks do not establish textual or historical accuracy. Bibliography claims require separate source-level examination.

evidenceAddendum.scope: All 79 Gospel events now contain individually written Scripture-context notes and 156 canonical comparison reading links. Targeted source-linked research issues additionally clarify census/Herod dating, the transmitted ending of Mark and ascension textual variants. The status of the historical audit remains a bounded editorial first pass.
evidenceAddendum.sourceLimit: Publisher academic abstracts (Oxford Handbook census and Cambridge New Testament Studies ascension) and ESV publisher manuscript footnotes were consulted. Complete subscription articles, original manuscript collation, independent historical specialist appraisal and independent archaeological identification were not performed. Full article access was not obtained.
evidenceAddendum.pending: The 79-event corpus has complete editorial reading-context coverage, but comprehensive specialist textual/archaeological corroboration, contested claims, site identifications and sitewide navigation quality assurance remain open.

siteReviewAddendum.scope: Reviewed the evidence classification and bibliography of all 35 Gospel geography dossiers, and added explicit research claim/evidence/limits assessments to five high-risk site identifications. Twelve region-only placeholders deliberately lack precise external site bibliography; that is not considered a broken citation.

siteReviewAddendum.limits: Publication abstracts, scholarly bibliographic descriptions and existing archaeological project summaries were consulted; full articles and original field datasets have not all been inspected. This does not amount to archaeologist certification or acceptance of one disputed site.
